newsitem.title: UK: Pesticides may cause Gulf War syndrome - Britain.
newsitem.headline: Pesticides may cause Gulf War syndrome - Britain.

text.p: Britain said on Friday pesticides used in the 1991 Gulf War could be linked to crippling illnesses suffered by veterans, popularly known as Gulf War Syndrome.

"The use of some OPs (organophosphate pesticides) may possibly be a clue to the conditions that some Gulf War veterans have suffered from," said Nicholas Soames, defence minister for the armed forces, in a statement.
"It will be investigated fully and with the utmost care."
The pesticides, some bought locally, were used to control insect-borne disease in the desert during the campaign.

Lawyers representing more than 1,000 former British servicemen suffering from the Syndrome welcomed the statement but expressed frustration that it had taken so long for the government to admit the possibility of a link with the pesticides.

"We can prove with documentation and witness statements that since 1991 the MoD (Defence Ministry) has known that organophosphates were used extensively by our servicemen, who were not supplied with any form of protective clothing," Hilary Meredith of the Gulf War Solicitors Action Group said.
"Why has it taken the MoD five years to admit what everyone knew was in fact the case," she added in a statement.

Britain has previously stated it believed Gulf War Syndrome did not exist and any ailments were caused by the stress of war. But it has investigated 750 Gulf veterans under a medical assessment programme launched three years ago.

Veterans say a "cocktail" of immunisations to protect them against chemical and biological warfare was the likely cause of symptoms including chronic fatigue, asthma and skin complaints. Some veterans are now confined to wheelchairs and claim their children have suffered birth defects.
About 51,000 Britons were involved in the war against Iraq following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.
Soames said that during a review of Gulf War operational and environmental conditions, it became clear that organophosphate pesticides were used more widely than had been believed.

Authority was given to purchase some OPs in the Gulf area because of the difficulty in delivering sufficient quantities of pesticides to the Gulf in the early stages of the war and the "overriding need" to protect the British frontline troops.

"The decision to use these pesticides was taken in the interests of protecting our troops, and it is important to recognise that this was an important factor in the remarkable control of disease in the Gulf War," Soames said in a letter to the chairman of a parliamentary defence committee.
While the government knew that one OP, malathion, was used, there was now evidence that three others -- dimethyl phosphorothionate, diazinon and azamathiphos -- were used.
"We are conducting urgent investigations into the extent of use of such pesticides and I will write to you once we have a clearer picture on this," Soames said.
David Clark, defence spokesman of the opposition Labour Party, accused the government of dragging its feet in investigating Gulf War Syndrome.
"This government all along has tried to sweep the issue under the carpet. It's like pulling teeth getting them to progress this investigation," he said.
In April American scientists said they had found that the combination of chemicals troops were exposed to in the Gulf had effects on animals similar to those experienced by veterans.
